abstract: The rapid warming of the Arctic is causing the growing season to expand and the climate to become more unpredictable. This scenario is intensifying a crucial trade-off arctic plants face: maximizing growth during the short growing season while avoiding freezes at the shoulder seasons. In response, ecotypes have evolved phenological behaviors that are finely tuned to their local climate, which often involves the use of photoperiod cues, especially in the fall. Under the rearrangement of temperature and light regimes, however, such phenological adaptations might prevent native plants from taking advantage of longer growing seasons. To test this phenological mechanism of local adaptation we used a decade-long reciprocal transplant experiment in Northern Alaska and observed the effects of seasonal light and temperature regimes on the leaf phenology of an arctic foundation species, Eriophorum vaginatum. We found that ecotypes rely heavily on site-specific photoperiod cues, but may also use temperature cues. These results indicate that local adaptation of this widespread species to local climates required the evolution of diverging phenological responses to seasonal changes in light. Because light cues will remain stable as the shoulder seasons expand, these adaptations are increasingly maladaptive, and could leave Eriophorum vulnerable to more competitive species.
